talks.title: Slop Engagement Operations - The Weird Web of an AI-Fueled SEO Spambot | SLEUTHCON 2025
talks.teaser: Presents slop Engagement Operations - The Weird Web of an AI-Fueled SEO Spambot | SLEUTHCON 2025 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Alex Delmont and Jim Walter of SentinelLabs present at SLEUTHCON on "Slop Engagement Operations," an AI-fueled SEO spam bot framework called Akira targeting small business websites.

Key Topics: Akira's Python-based website scraping and content generation; OpenAI API abuse for customized spam; CAPTCHA bypass automation; hardcoded credentials in scripts; and multi-operator framework variants.

Technical Details: Researchers describe Akira scraping target websites, using Chat Completions API to generate tailored SEO spam content, and automating CAPTCHA defeat across reCAPTCHA and custom implementations. Credentials were hardcoded in plaintext across operator variants.

Takeaways: LLM-powered spam frameworks represent a new class of abuse tooling. Defenders should monitor for AI-generated content injection and protect against automated CAPTCHA-defeating submission attacks.

talks.title: Keynote | SLEUTHCON 2025
talks.teaser: Analyzes keynote | SLEUTHCON 2025 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Defining Crimeware

Paul Melson's SleuthCon keynote traces financially motivated crimeware—purpose-built software used to generate illegal revenue—distinguishing it from espionage, hacktivism, or generic malware that lacks direct monetization. The session blends history with lessons for modern defenders.

Professional Networks for Hunting

Before the historical survey, Melson argues professional relationships are undervalued for threat hunting—not just job searches. No individual possesses all data, skills, or ideas needed to disrupt criminal ecosystems at scale; collaboration across the community multiplies impact.

Early Eras of Digital Crime

He revisits dial-up-era scams including premium 900-number fraud and trojanized "copy protection" programs. One investigation traced a $9.95 campaign using a valid VeriSign code-signing certificate impersonating a legitimate client to a likely Las Vegas front company—what he calls early American crimeware.

Botnets and Patterns

The narrative continues through IRC botnets and evolving distribution models. Melson seeks recurring patterns across decades that might inform better defenses today, framing the talk as nostalgia with analytical purpose rather than pure storytelling.

talks.title: Bulletproof Hoster or Proxy Provider? Wrong - It’s Both, or Even More. | SLEUTHCON 2025
talks.teaser: Demonstrates bulletproof Hoster or Proxy Provider? Wrong - Its Both, or Even More. | SLEUTHCON 2025 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Mapping bulletproof providers

Ste, a Team Cymru threat researcher, reframes his Sleuthcon talk as lessons on bulletproof hosting and proxy abuse. He outlines underground forums, jurisdiction-shopping operators, and comparison-site-listed providers that enable crime without advertising it openly.

PSB Hosting case study

He walks through PSB Hosting, a Russian-linked operator UK-incorporated in 2024, traced via Companies House, a leaked phone number, Apios OSINT, Discord/Telegram aliases, and personal Telegram activity including crypto and biking posts.

Proxy infrastructure scale

Team Cymru maps AS/netblocks tagged as proxies—about 10,000 IPs for PSB alone—linked to resellers like RapidSeedbox, IPRoyal, and SigmaProxy, with Leaseweb Netherlands colocation appearing in the chain. He notes 16 million newly tagged proxy IPs in one week, making attribution and blocking difficult.

talks.title: Up the Garden Path: Applying Cyber Deception to the Attack Lifecycle | SLEUTHCON 2025
talks.teaser: Examines up the Garden Path: Applying Cyber Deception to the Attack Lifecycle | SLEUTHCON 2025 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Deception as behavior design

The speaker defines cyber deception as influencing financially motivated attackers' decisions and resulting actions—a dynamic "see, think, do" loop rather than static tripwires. Effective programs scale by focusing on recorded behaviors observed in the environment, not passive honeypots alone.

Recon through lateral movement

At recon, deploy discoverable sock-puppet personas mirroring real OSINT targets—verify they appear in the same search tools adversaries use. For initial access scenarios like phishing, seed plausible breach credentials. Internal SharePoint and Confluence documents can be SEO-tuned so decoy artifacts rank in search results insiders and attackers browse.

Garden path narrative example

A fictional sysadmin "James" publishes honeypot documents about "dog food optimization servers," leading attackers into high-fidelity traps. The approach prioritizes alert fidelity over noisy VM-scanner hits, taking decisive action only when adversaries engage curated deception assets across the attack lifecycle.
